Beauty’s fastest-growing markets have one thing in common …. and it isn’t geography.

The Big Question:
If eCommerce is projected to outpace every other beauty channel across nearly every major region, what does that mean for how brands allocate investment over the next five years?

By the Numbers:
• Africa: eComm projected to grow 33.5% CAGR (2025–2030)

• Middle East: 16.3% CAGR

• Latin America: 15.8% CAGR

• North America: eCommerce 6.8% CAGR, while department stores are projected to decline 3.7%

Why It Matters:
The common thread across these markets is not geography, income levels, or retail maturity. It is that eCommerce is expected to be the fastest-growing beauty channel almost everywhere!!!

That has downstream implications well beyond online sales. As more consumer journeys begin digitally, competitive advantage increasingly depends on stronger content, retail media execution, marketplace strategy, and digital shelf performance.

Brands that continue to treat eCommerce as a supporting channel risk underinvesting in the capabilities that will drive future growth.

What I Would Do:
1/ Shift planning from channel-first to consumer-first. Invest where consumers are increasingly discovering, researching, and buying.

2/ Build digital shelf excellence, retail media, content, and marketplace strategy as one connected growth engine instead of separate initiatives.

3/ Increase investment in high-growth international markets where digital commerce is accelerating fastest while continuing to strengthen execution in mature markets.

4/ Leverage Pattern to accelerate marketplace growth, improve digital shelf performance, and scale globally with a proven eCommerce operating model.

TLDR:
The biggest opportunity in beauty is not limited to one region. It is the continued shift toward digital commerce. Brands that organize around that reality today will be better positioned for tomorrow.

I was wrong. I am.

The media company is Tenex Media. It's the digital destination for AI education & applied AI, and it sits on top of Tenex, the applied AI consultancy & lab my cofounder & I launched 15 months ago.

We're actively hiring for key founding team roles at Tenex Media, which I'll share below.

And in sharing these roles, you'll also get a sense of our strategy—what feels like lessons learned from Morning Brew & what feels like new, unexplored territory.

1) We're hiring 2-3 Full-Stack AI Creators.

Personality-driven content is becoming a bigger and bigger part of consumers’ media diets. The democratization of creation & distribution means that people can attract as much attention as institutions & consumers have always longed for content that feels personal/relatable.

And we're seeing this take shape in the AI space with personalities like Andrej Karpathy, Boris Cherny, @signulll, Aaron Levie, Arvind Jain and others.

You have maybe the best job in the world as a full-stack AI creator. You build with AI. You talk about what you build. You teach people how to use AI through content. And you train F2000 enterprises on AI.

Brand-driven content isn’t dead. The expectations of it have just changed & it serves a more important role in media than ever before.

There is one foundation, two channels & three franchises that you will own in your role.

The foundation: the content machine. We've developed an internal AI system that allows us to create editorial at scale without sacrificing voice or quality. You will use & improve the content machine to become a one-person wrecking ball.

Two channels: website and newsletter. 30% of our inbound MQLS in Q2 came from AEO. That's crazy because we haven't done jack shit to optimize our website or long-form content. Next, is newsletter. I'm a little biased. But great editorial newsletters have never been more important to own & nurture your audience. You'll take our newsletter, Ultrathink, from 1x to 3x per week and make it the best applied AI newsletter in the world.

Franchises:

Content Engineering is to modern marketing what DevOps was to software. A new discipline that makes scale, governance, and speed possible without sacrificing craft.

posts.content:
Five market leaders. One regional winner.

Shopee’s H1 2026 Makeup brand rankings across six Southeast Asian markets reveal an important distinction:
Winning one country and winning Southeast Asia are two different jobs.

Across Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore, five different brands ranked No.1:
Indonesia: Oh My Glam
Thailand: Maybelline
Vietnam: 3CE
Malaysia: Glad2Glow
Philippines: Maybelline
Singapore: Skintific

But when sales within all six Top 100 samples are combined, Maybelline becomes the clear regional leader at RMB 267.1M—almost twice the sales of No.2 Skintific at RMB 138.7M.

The reason is not dominance in one large market.

It is consistency across all six:
No.2 in Indonesia
No.1 in Thailand
No.3 in Vietnam
No.5 in Malaysia
No.1 in the Philippines
No.5 in Singapore

Maybelline was the only brand to rank in the Top 5 in every market. It also recorded positive YoY growth across all six, translating into approximately 20% combined growth within the sample.

That consistency is rare.

The six rankings contained 369 distinct brands:
269 brands—73%—appeared in only one market
Only 9 brands—2%—entered the Top 100 in all six
Only one brand remained in the Top 5 everywhere

This changes how regional leadership should be measured.

A local No.1 position proves that a brand can win a market. It does not prove that the same strength can travel.

For regional makeup teams, the more useful questions are:
How many markets place the brand near the top?
Is performance dependent on one large country?
Can the brand remain relevant across different price points and competitive sets?
Is growth broad-based—or concentrated in one local peak?

In Southeast Asia Makeup, local leadership creates headlines. Consistency across markets creates regional scale.

The H1 takeaway for brands is clear:
Do not measure Southeast Asia only by the markets you win. Measure how consistently you compete across the markets you enter.

Data source: NWi跨境通
Scope: Shopee Makeup Top 100 brands across Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore; January–June 2026; ranked by sales revenue, RMB. Regional brand sales and growth are calculated from each market’s Top 100 sample.
#Makeup #SoutheastAsia #Shopee #BeautyIndustry #Ecommerce #Maybelline

posts.content:
My dog made a mess in the hallway this week (I'll spare you the details).

But I asked AI for some product recommendations. Then, for fun, I asked four more.

Same question, word for word: best dog probiotic for a sudden sensitive stomach 😬

I expected a little nuance. That isn't what I got.

𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧: Nutramax Proviable (then talked itself into FortiFlora when I pushed)
𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘁𝘆: Purina FortiFlora
𝗚𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶: Purina FortiFlora
𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲: Purina FortiFlora
𝗔𝗺𝗮𝘇𝗼𝗻'𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴: Purina FortiFlora. "Vet's #1 Recommended," add-to-cart button included.

An entire category. One unanimous winner.

𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝘇𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼👇

I asked each AI WHY. The sources that created the winner:

🔹 𝗣𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗮'𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲: Perplexity told me straight out it leaned on "FortiFlora's own product information."
🔹 𝗣𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗮'𝘀 𝘃𝗲𝘁-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝘂𝗯: cited 3 times by Gemini
🔹 𝗣𝗲𝘁𝗠𝗗: cited by nearly all of them
🔹 And a pile of blogs you've never heard of: iHeartDogs, PawOrigins, HappyDogGut

Not review count. No bestseller rank. Not ad spend or conversion rate.

The brand that published the clinical content became the answer everywhere. And it could come from their own outlets.

And where do the AIs send you to buy? PetSmart. Walmart. Petco.

Amazon got ONE mention across the four outside assistants. The listing you've spent years optimizing is potentially invisible in this funnel.

One more thing. In Amazon's AI, a brand appeared in the answer with a "Sponsored" tag.

Sponsored placements inside AI conversations are live, which is a whole other conversation.

The old playbook: win the search results page.
The new one: win the citations, or buy the seat while you still can.

Run this for your category.

Five AIs, one key question, ten minutes. If they all crown a brand and it isn't yours, you didn't lose a ranking fight. You lost a citation fight you didn't know was happening.

(The dog is fine. The hallway has seen things.)

#ai #ecommerce #marketing #amazonads

Amazon Beauty Q2 2026: Medicube overtakes skincare’s legacy leaders

In April, I wrote that medicube was on track to become Amazon’s top skincare brand by mid-2026. Pattern, the global e-commerce accelerator, now puts Medicube at 4.1% of Amazon skincare sales, up 0.6pts from Q1. The Korean brand moved from third to first, ahead of La Roche-Posay at 3.5%, down 0.2pts. CeraVe, the Q1 leader, fell to third at 2.7% after losing 1.3pts. Medicube now leads La Roche-Posay by 0.6pts and CeraVe by 1.4pts. My forecast was right, but I did not expect the change to happen so quickly.

The top ten skincare brands accounted for 22.3% of sales, down 0.2pts from Q1. Neutrogena held fourth at 2.4%, while The Ordinary remained fifth at 2.1%. EltaMD made the largest move below the leaders, climbing from ninth to sixth after gaining 0.7pts to reach 2.0%.

In makeup, established leaders lost ground to challengers brands. The top ten’s combined share fell from 31.4% to 29.2%, a decline of 2.2pts. The ranking was unchanged through sixth place, but every top-five brand lost share. Maybelline remained first at 4.8%, narrowly ahead of L’Oréal Paris at 4.6%. E.l.f. recorded the largest decline among the leaders, losing 0.7pts to reach 3.9%. Tarte was the top ten’s strongest grower. It gained 0.5pts and moved from tenth to seventh with a 2.3% share. Grande Cosmetics fell from seventh to ninth, while Revlon returned at 1.6%, replacing Babe Original.

Fragrance continued to concentrate. The top ten reached 31.0% of sales, up from 29.9% in Q1. Lattafa extended its lead to 7.3%, while Versace remained second at 4.6%. Yves Saint Laurent rose from fifth to third at 2.9%, and Armani Beauty climbed from seventh to fifth after gaining 0.5pts. Dolce & Gabbana entered the ranking at 1.8%, replacing Afnan. Afnan leaving the top ten and Armaf loosing a position while Lattafa strengthened its lead suggests Middle Eastern fragrance is consolidating rather than advancing across the board. Meanwhile, L’Oréal’s luxury brands gained ground on Amazon with the good performance of Saint Laurent and Armani.

Haircare remained the least concentrated category, with the top ten’s share rising slightly from 16.3% to 16.7%. Nutrafol and Redken retained the first two positions at 3.1% and 2.0%. TYMO was the quarter’s fastest grower. Its share increased by 0.6pts to 1.9%, moving the brand from eighth to third place. Olaplex fell from third to fifth, while Wavytalk moved from tenth to eighth. Color Wow dropped four places to ninth. Finally, Kérastase returned to the top ten at 1.2%, replacing Amika.

posts.content:
If you already know where you want to end up, your entire career before the MBA should be designed backwards.

For example:
→ If your dream is Private Equity, the strongest trajectory is often:
Investment Banking or MBB → Wharton/Harvard → Private Equity → PE Partner.

→ If you want to build the next billion-dollar startup:
Founder or Big Tech → Stanford → Founder again.

→ If you want to become a global product leader:
Software Engineering or Product Management → Stanford/MIT → VP Product → Chief Product Officer.

→ If your goal is Fortune 500 leadership:
Consulting or Corporate Strategy → Harvard/Kellogg → General Management → CEO.

→ If Venture Capital is your destination:
Founder, Product, or MBB → Stanford → VC → General Partner.

The most important question isn't where you are today. It's where you want to be 15–20 years from now.

Once that destination is crystal clear, today's decisions become much easier.

Which job should you take?
Should you switch industries?
Should you pursue leadership opportunities?
Should you build a startup?
Should you even do an MBA, and if yes, which one?

The answers start revealing themselves.

Clarity of destination creates clarity of action. And clarity of action creates extraordinary outcomes.

#MBA #GROWTH

posts.content:
I just realized why my LinkedIn posts get unusually high engagement rates.  And it's really easy to do, once you know it. So I thought I'd share.

Whenever I'm working on a new post, I ask myself: What would I comment on this post, if it came up on my feed?

If I can't think of a good answer - an easy comment I'd throw out there - I keep working.

I do this automatically so I didn't actually notice I was doing it.

Until I recently read 400+ underperforming posts (client project, long story) and found myself saying "What do they think anyone could POSSIBLY reply to this?" over and over again.

Some posts come with an easy response built in:

- Asking for advice/recommendations
- Job announcements
- Complaining about a shared pain point
- Anything with a dog in it :)

But you can apply this to anything. And you don't have to do the whole "Comment [engagement bait] below and I'll send it to you" schtick either.

For instance, if I'm sharing some advice, I'll often ask people to join in and share a tip in the comments. I'm not doing this just to trick people into engaging, because A) that grosses me out completely and b) I really like the idea of making my posts more valuable to the reader by getting more suggestions in the comments c) selfishly I do actually want to learn new tips myself :)

But it has a nice side effect of sometimes encouraging engagement. A lot of people enjoy giving useful advice when they can.

I don't know if that's really the reason my engagements are up 600% over last year. Could be a lot of things.  But it's my best guess.

What do you think? 😉

OK, I did that to make the point but I am also genuinely curious, so please do humor me :) What gets engagement up on your posts? Have you seen engagement go up or down lately? Do you think my diagnosis of what works sounds right?

posts.content:
$325M for a stain remover that hands 40 cents of every dollar straight to Amazon.

Everything you've been told about DTC says this brand should have sold cheap.
It went for 11.6x EBITDA.

Last week Church & Dwight Co., Inc. , closed its acquisition of @Miss mouth' The #1 stain remover on Amazon. ~90,000 reviews. $80M in sales, $28M in EBITDA.

That's a 35% EBITDA margin on an Amazon-native brand. Sit with that.

Reverse-engineer the P&L and it looks roughly like this:
→ 80% product margin (it's a spray bottle of stain remover)
→ ~40% of revenue eaten by Amazon fees, fulfillment and ppc
→ Just 5% in operating expenses
→ 35% drops to EBITDA

Here's what most people miss. That 40% "Amazon tax" everyone fears? It replaced an entire company. No warehouse. No logistics team. No 30-person media-buying department. No finance org. They rent Amazon's machine and still keep a third of revenue as profit.

Most "independent" $80M DTC brands the ones bleeding on Meta CAC and 3PL fees would kill for half that margin.

Now the part nobody's saying out loud.

Miss Mouth's was a Thrasio brand.
Yes, that Thrasio. The aggregator that raised billions rolling up Amazon brands and filed for bankruptcy in 2024. They picked up Miss Mouth's back in 2020 for a fraction of $325M most estimates put it under $10M.

The aggregator graveyard just produced a nine-figure exit.

The lesson for operators:
Channel concentration is supposed to be a valuation discount. Here it wasn't. Because 90,000 reviews and repeat purchase prove the revenue is real demand, not rented traffic. A strategic will happily pay 11.6x for "risky" Amazon revenue when the unit economics show a brand, not an ad campaign.
So which is the better $80M business  the independent one scrapping for 15% margins, or the Amazon-dependent one printing 35%?

Church & Dwight just told you which one they'd write the check for.

Would you?

The brands winning AI recommendations today are likely to win consumer consideration tomorrow.

As consumers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, and Google AI what products they should buy, a new battleground is emerging. It is no longer just about ranking on Google or winning shelf space. It is about becoming the brand AI is most likely to recommend.

The Big Question:
If AI becomes the first place consumers ask for beauty advice, is your brand showing up in the answer?

By the Numbers:
🔥 7.0% - The Ordinary leads estimated AI citations
🔥 6.0% - CeraVe
🔥 5.5% - Sephora
🔥 5.0% - La Roche-Posay
🔥 4.5% - Charlotte Tilbury

Why It Matters:
Generative AI is becoming another discovery channel. Every recommendation reflects the information AI can access about a brand, including product data, reviews, expert content, retailer information, and broader digital authority.

This is not traditional SEO. It is a new optimization challenge where trust, structured content, and high quality signals influence whether your brand is recommended or ignored.

For beauty brands, where shoppers frequently ask questions about skin type, routines, ingredients, and product comparisons, AI recommendations could shape millions of purchase decisions over the next few years.

What I Would Do:
1/ Audit the prompts your consumers are asking across major AI platforms.

2/ Measure which brands are consistently recommended and understand why.

3/ Invest in product content, reviews, expert credibility, and structured data that AI models can confidently reference.

4/ Partner with Pattern to build an AI visibility strategy alongside your marketplace and retail media investments.

TLDR:
Winning search was the last decade’s challenge.

Winning AI recommendations may become this decade’s competitive advantage.

Turns out the company blog was a lease, not an asset.

State of Brand published a piece making this case and the numbers are rough. Under a third of Google searches end in a click to any website now, the sharpest jump in zero-click behavior in a decade. Search traffic to publishers fell 33% in a year. LinkedIn company pages reach about 1.6% of their followers, down from 7% in 2021.

So both channels B2B marketing leaned on for fifteen years are shrinking at the same time, and most teams' response so far has been to post harder.

The more interesting response, and the one the piece makes a real case for, is becoming a publisher. Industry news, interviews with the practitioners you actually want as customers, quick takes on the stories your market cares about.

The pipeline angle is even more compelling. When the people you interview are your buyers, you get warm relationships and free distribution out of the same conversation. They share the piece, their network reads it, some of them call you.

And the bar to start is low. One writer, a section of your existing site, a narrow focus on where your brand genuinely has something worth saying. Treat LinkedIn as the delivery truck, not the store.

Algorithms will keep moving the goalposts. A reader who comes to you directly is the only one nobody can take away.

Read the full piece on State of Brand: https://lnkd.in/g-cEZ_Y9
